standard.title: Movement concepts
standard.description: demonstrate how movement concepts related to effort, space, time, objects and people can be applied when performing movement sequences
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have investigated different ways of moving their body and manipulating objects and space (AC9HP2M02). They have explored movement in an experimental way but have not yet applied named movement concepts deliberately in sequences.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students demonstrate how movement concepts related to effort, space, time, objects and people can be applied when performing movement sequences.

nodes.label: Effort concepts — acceleration, deceleration, direction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can demonstrate acceleration, deceleration and changing direction of movement in minor games and rhythmic or expressive activities.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate acceleration, deceleration and direction change in at least one minor game or movement activity, and label each when prompted.
nodes.typical_width: Demonstrate and name effort concepts across minor games and rhythmic/expressive activities; explain how varying effort achieves different movement outcomes.
wider: Explore how acceleration and deceleration are used strategically in a chosen sport (e.g. to evade an opponent or close a gap) and demonstrate an application.
Compose a short expressive movement phrase in which effort changes (fast/slow, strong/light) are the deliberate communication tool.
nodes.hinge_reason: Effort concepts (especially acceleration/deceleration and direction change) are the foundation for strategic movement in games contexts. Students who cannot execute deliberate effort changes cannot meaningfully demonstrate space and time concepts in node 2, because spatial manipulation depends on timed effort shifts.

response_modes.reason: Students often experience effort changes without naming them. Explicit labelling practice — calling out 'accelerate', 'decelerate', 'change direction' during activity — builds the conceptual vocabulary needed for deliberate application.

success_criteria: Demonstrates deliberate acceleration, deceleration or direction change in a movement activity.
Labels at least two effort concepts when observing or performing movement.
Explains how changing effort helped them achieve a movement outcome.

nodes.label: Space concepts — levels, pathways, flow
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss and demonstrate different levels, movement pathways and use of space and flow in movement sequences.
nodes.minimum_width: Perform a movement sequence that uses at least two different levels or pathways, and describe the spatial choices made.
nodes.typical_width: Design and perform a movement sequence that deliberately uses levels, pathways, space and flow as compositional tools; discuss the effect of spatial choices on the sequence.
wider: Analyse how different dance forms or gymnastic styles use levels and pathways as expressive elements and incorporate one observed spatial pattern into their own sequence.
Create a movement map (diagram or annotated sketch) showing the levels and pathways in their sequence, then modify the sequence and update the map.

response_modes.reason: Spatial concepts apply differently in dance, gymnastics, and games contexts. Experiencing the same concepts across contexts builds richer and more flexible spatial understanding.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Levels, pathways and flow have rich cross-context pedagogical potential — expressive in dance, functional in games, structural in gymnastics. Wider exploration across these contexts deepens conceptual understanding significantly.
success_criteria: Demonstrates at least two different spatial elements (level, pathway or use of space) in a movement sequence.
Describes the spatial choices made and explains why those choices were made.
Identifies where flow (smooth vs sudden transitions) occurs in their sequence.

nodes.label: Body awareness — symmetry, shapes, angles
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use their body to demonstrate symmetry, shapes and angles when performing movement skills, balances or sequences.
nodes.minimum_width: Perform at least one movement or balance that demonstrates a named body shape (e.g. tuck, straddle, straight, star) and identify the symmetry or angle involved.
nodes.typical_width: Perform a range of movements and balances that demonstrate symmetrical and asymmetrical shapes, different angles and contrasting body shapes; describe the body awareness used in each.
wider: Explore how body shape concepts connect to geometric concepts (lines of symmetry, angles as degrees) and demonstrate a sequence where body shapes are described using mathematical language.
Investigate how specific performance styles (e.g. classical ballet, gymnastics, First Nations Australian dance) use body shape as a primary expressive or technical element.

response_modes.reason: Students need to build a vocabulary of named body shapes and positions (tuck, pike, straddle, straight, wide, narrow) to access more complex composition and performance tasks. Accumulating a repertoire of demonstrated shapes is the primary investment here.

success_criteria: Names and demonstrates at least three different body shapes.
Identifies whether a movement or balance is symmetrical or asymmetrical.
Uses the term 'angle' correctly when describing a body position.

nodes.label: Manipulating space in games contexts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore different ways of manipulating space to receive passes, maintain possession, or increase or decrease scoring opportunities in games.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate one spatial strategy in a game (e.g. moving to create space, closing space defensively) and explain what they were trying to achieve.
nodes.typical_width: Demonstrate spatial manipulation strategies across at least two game categories (invasion, net/court, striking/fielding or target games); explain how space manipulation connects to the scoring or possession outcome.
wider: Analyse a game play (observed or played) to identify how both teams are using space manipulation — mapping movements and explaining the spatial battle.
Design a small-sided game modification that forces a particular type of space manipulation (e.g. a constraint that limits defending space) and explain its intended effect.
nodes.hinge_reason: Spatial manipulation in games is the integrative application that demonstrates the full movement concepts standard. Without this applied understanding, the concepts of effort, space, time, objects and people remain disconnected from the games literacy demanded at Y5-6 (AC9HP6M03).

response_modes.reason: This node draws together effort (when to move), space (where to move), time (how quickly) and people (relative to teammates and opponents). Teacher investment should focus on helping students connect these concepts rather than treating each separately.
Spatial manipulation works differently across game categories. Students who have only experienced invasion game space concepts may have limited transfer to target or net/court contexts.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Game category breadth (invasion, net/court, target, striking/fielding) is the primary enrichment axis here — the spatial logic differs substantially across categories, making cross-category experience genuinely valuable.
success_criteria: Identifies a spatial opportunity or problem in a game and names a strategy to address it.
Demonstrates deliberate space manipulation (creating or closing space) in a game.
Explains how their spatial movement affected a scoring or possession outcome.
